q: A test for difficult intubation has a sensitivity of 60% and specificity of 90%. In a population where 10% are difficult to intubate, what is the positive predictive value?
why: In 1000 patients: 100 difficult; true positives = 60, false negatives = 40. Of 900 not difficult, false positives = 90 (10%), true negatives = 810. PPV = 60/(60+90) = 40%. NPV = 810/850 ≈ 95%. PPV depends on prevalence, whereas sensitivity and specificity do not.

q: On a forest plot, what does it mean when the diamond (pooled estimate) does not cross the line of no effect?
o: The pooled result is statistically significant
why: Each square is a study's point estimate (size reflects weight) with horizontal lines for confidence intervals. The diamond's width shows the pooled confidence interval; if it does not cross the line of no effect (1 for ratios, 0 for differences), the result is statistically significant. Heterogeneity is assessed by I² and the chi-squared test; funnel plots look for publication bias.

q: Which type of bias is minimised by allocation concealment in a randomised controlled trial?
why: Allocation concealment stops investigators knowing the next allocation, preventing selective enrolment (selection bias). Blinding reduces performance and detection bias; intention-to-treat analysis and complete follow-up reduce attrition bias; trial registration addresses publication bias. Recall bias affects case–control studies.

q: Researchers compare length of stay (skewed data) between two independent groups of patients. Which test is most appropriate?
why: For non-normally distributed continuous or ordinal data in two independent groups, use the Mann–Whitney U test; for paired non-parametric data, Wilcoxon signed-rank. Normally distributed data use unpaired or paired t-tests (ANOVA for three or more groups). Chi-squared or Fisher's exact test compares proportions of categorical data.
